title: Logging and metrics causing GIL contention on small requests (audit)
body:
Summary:

Quick audit of an observed tail-latency spike for very small requests (payload < 1KB) that correlates with periods of high metrics/log throughput. Hypothesis is that synchronous logging/metrics emission under the Python GIL is adding non-trivial per-request CPU cost and creating contention that shows up in 95/99th percentile latency.

Context / why we care:
- Small, latency-sensitive requests (chat ping, rerank health-check type) should be cheap. We observed 95p latency regressions from ~12ms -> 35–60ms under load bursts.
- This workload is common for customers who do many short queries; unit economics and SLOs are impacted.

Notable signals that led to this audit:
- Flamegraphs sampled during tail spikes show repeated Python frame stacks inside logging.emit and metrics client flush functions.
- strace-like sampling shows occasional write(2) syscalls for collecting/serializing metrics right on request path.
- pprof-like CPU samples show a cluster at the GIL-holding frames when spikes occur.
- Metric ingestion rate aligns with bursts: ~10k metrics/s across worker processes at peak.

Observations (raw):
- On a 16-vCPU box with 8 workers, baseline small-request p50=10ms p95=13ms p99=18ms. During metric burst p95 jumps to 40ms, p99 to >100ms (single observed instance ~220ms).
- Sampling profiler (3s, 100Hz) during a spike: ~27% samples in logging.Logger._log -> logging.Handler.emit; ~18% in metrics_client.flush (synchronous path).
- Many of the logging frames show format string interpolation happening in Python before handler call, indicating work done while holding GIL.
- Worker thread dumps show other workers blocked on PyGILState_Ensure or waiting to acquire the interpreter lock.
- The metrics client uses a synchronous TCP/HTTP emit for internal telemetry with a small buffer; when buffer full it will flush during request processing.

Hypotheses / root causes to consider:
1) Synchronous logging and metrics serialization and I/O happening on the request-handling thread while holding the GIL.
2) Synchronous flushes triggered by buffer thresholds or by background timer coordination that races with incoming requests.
3) Logging formatters and extra fields allocate objects (str, dict) and run Python code under the GIL, increasing GC pressure and blocking other threads.
4) C-extension metrics path exists but falls back to pure-Python when configuration/environment differs (e.g., dev container), causing variability.

Experiments run so far (notes):
- Experiment A: Disabled structured logging formatters (switched to a very cheap lambda -> preformatted str). Result: p95 reduced ~20% during bursts.
- Experiment B: Replaced blocking metrics_client.emit with a stub that enqueues to a bounded multiprocessing.Queue consumed by a separate process (no network IO on request path). Result: p95 returned near-baseline, p99 improved but occasional spikes remained.
- Experiment C: Enabled non-blocking UDP sink for internal metrics (best-effort). Result: similar to B but with some lost metrics; operationally acceptable for internal debug metrics.
- Experiment D: Instrumented to force metrics client to use C-extension fastpath. Result: improved but still saw serialization cost on Python side.

More detailed microbenchmarks:
- Time to log a simple preformatted string (no interpolation) under current handler: ~0.12ms median, 95p 0.3ms.
- Time to call metrics_client.emit that does local JSON serialization + socket send: median 0.35ms, 95p 0.9ms.
- JSON serialization (json.dumps on small dict) median 0.18ms 95p 0.6ms.
- PyObject creation for structured logging (format, extras) accounts for ~30–40% of total wall time for the path in microbench.

Unresolved questions / gotchas:
- Some forks/build variants use a different metrics library that relies on requests (blocking) vs the C-extension: need to audit wheel/build matrix.
- Is the metrics sink sometimes blocked because downstream collector is slow, causing synchronous backpressure? Need to check collector logs.
- Are we double-serializing in some code paths (e.g., format -> handler creates JSON string then handler wraps into envelope)?

Proposed mitigations (ranked):
1) Short term (low-risk): Offload metric/log emit to an asynchronous worker per-process (dedicated thread) using a lock-free queue or ringbuffer. Keep enqueuing non-blocking and drop when full. This removes network IO from request path and reduces GIL hold time for emission.
2) Medium term: Move heavy formatting (structured fields) to the background worker; on request path only capture minimal precomputed identifiers and timestamps.
3) Medium term: Provide a C-extension fastpath for critical serialization (small JSON blobs) to avoid Python object churn; fallback still allowed.
4) Long term: Adopt a non-blocking low-overhead metrics protocol on the in-process path (binary compact encoding, preallocated buffers), and ensure handler does not call blocking syscalls while holding GIL.
5) Operational: Add runtime config toggle to disable internal debug logs/metrics flush under high QPS to preserve SLOs and surface as customer-configurable.

Proposed rollout plan / quick patch idea:
- Patch PR (prototype): replace metrics_client.emit call sites in request path with metrics_client.enqueue(metric) and spin up a background thread per worker that drains queue and performs actual emission. Add bounded queue size with drop semantics and stat counters for dropped metrics. Target small diff (~10 LOC per callsite) and run perf canary. (Linked PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serve/pull/1829)
- Canary: deploy to a small Dedicated pool for 48h, compare p95/p99 on small-request synthetic load and customer traffic.
- If successful, roll to more pools.

Metrics to evaluate success:
- 95th and 99th latency for <=1KB requests under synthetic injection and production-like traffic.
- CPU profile sampling showing reduced samples in logging.emit and metrics.flush frames.
- Observe queue drop metrics and downstream ingestion counts to ensure we are not dropping critical signals.

Notes on instrumentation used:
- linux perf + py-spy 0.3 for sampling stacks (safe for production, low overhead).
- in-prod micro-sampler running 1s cpu captures every 10s during tests.
- naive strace on a reproduction box to confirm write(2) occurrences aligned with request handling.

Next steps (actionable):
1) Continue with the background-queue patch and get a small canary (Ravi + Ben to own test infra).
2) Audit packaging matrix for metrics fastpath C-extension (Sofia to follow up).
3) Add a lightweight runtime flag for 'emit-offload' and default to on in Dedicated/Hosted.
4) Add a perf regression test in CI that runs microbench with logging+metrics enabled and asserts p95 under threshold.
5) Re-run sampled flamegraphs post-rollback to confirm reduction in GIL-held frames.

Notes to reviewers / open asks:
- We need a quick decision on acceptable drop semantics for internal metrics during bursts. Is losing 2–5% of internal debug metrics acceptable vs SLO risk?
- We should confirm compliance/observability needs (audit logs must still be durable). Suggest policy: keep security/audit logs synchronous and move debug/telemetry to async.

Appendix (breadcrumbs):
- Local repro: tools/perf-repro/small-req-metrics-burst.py (script used for synthetic load)
- Profiler outputs stored at s3://redwood-perf/logging-gil-audit/2025-10-18/
- Related tickets: RT-5342 (root), RT-5381 (metrics collector backpressure investigation)

Rough timeline: 1 week for prototype + canary, 2–3 weeks for medium-term rollout and CI tests, longer for C-extension work.

Notes-to-self: capture a couple of stacks showing logging.format -> logging.emit while holding GIL to paste into the PR; include sample perf flamegraph as png in the PR description.
